title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
content: At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. "I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. He has little doubt they are dead. But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death. But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. "In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. "Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. "We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required. The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn). At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy. Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects. Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming. "When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders. This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster. For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar. He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati. But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village. Once again, he is without a home. "I have lost everything," he said. So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal. Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies. He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home. Additional reporting: Rajneesh Bhandari Opposition leaders have alleged that CEC Gyanesh Kumar manipulated voter rolls to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party during elections. Police have said it is “strongly suspected” that the incident was caused by a gas leak. Schmidt acknowledged that his actions "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt". Anojan Sivarasa faces execution after he was found guilty of blasphemy over a Facebook comment. Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock. The article's focus on the human cost of the disaster makes it a significant event that requires attention.

title: US resident arrested in connection with deadly British Columbia school shooting
content: A 30-year-old US resident has been arrested in connection with a deadly school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, for allegedly encouraging the suspect, authorities said. James Cody Bryant was charged in the state of Washington with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, the US Department of Justice said. Bryant "had been in repeated contact with the shooter, offering advice, sending money, and even agreeing to livestream a horrific event," officials said. Eight people, including six children, were killed in the February attack, one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. Authorities said it was carried out by Jessie Van Rootselaar, 18, a resident of the town. Bryant had the "information and ability to alert law enforcement, and even discussed that possibility with the suspect, but chose not to", acting US Attorney Neil Floyd said during a joint news conference with Canadian authorities on Tuesday. The 30-year-old faces a penalty of up to life in prison if found guilty, officials said. The shooting occurred at Van Rootselaar's home and at a secondary school in Tumbler Ridge, a town of 2,300 residents. Van Roostelaar died of a self-inflicted gunshot injury during the attack. Bryant allegedly enabled the suspect over a period of months, providing technical advice, money, and items to be used in the attack, Mike Herrington, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Seattle, said. The Washington resident also agreed to record and broadcast a livestream of the attack in a way that would "maximise notoriety for the shooter", Herrington said. The stream was online for only about 20 seconds and was viewed by one account, according to court documents. "Without Bryant's misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the livestream, we don't ultimately know if the shooter would have gone through with the crime," Herrington said, alleging that Bryant was fully aware of when the attack began. A 41-page federal complaint against Bryant includes photos and text messages authorities said were sent to and from Van Rootselaar. According to federal law enforcement, the pair met three years ago online, losing touch twice while Van Rootselaar was admitted to a mental health facility. They communicated daily on the app Discord in the six months before the mass shooting. They discussed, among other things, sending 3D-printed weapons over the US-Canada border. The text messages appeared to show that Bryant initially suggested targeting a shopping centre instead of a school. Bryant also told the shooter to delay or not commit the attack at some point during their conversations but ultimately told Van Rootselaar, they would not "snitch" to the police. Police said Van Rootselaar was known to law enforcement due to a history of mental health-related visits over the years to the suspect's home. Van Rootselaar's mother and 11-year-old stepbrother were killed in the February shooting, along with five young children and an educator at the school. Several lawsuits have since been filed in relation to the attack. After it was revealed that Van Roostelaar had consulted ChatGPT prior to the attack, the province of British Columbia, as well as some families of the victims, sued tech giant OpenAI for allegedly failing to notify authorities about the shooter's interactions with the chatbot. In April, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman apologised to the families of the victims. "I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement," Altman wrote in an open letter. Experts and lawyers called the apparent recovery unprecedented, noting she is believed to be the only known person to survive a lethal injection. The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions. The BBC's Samira Hussain explains the impact the $110bn merger will have on consumers of both entertainment giants. The BBC speaks to experts about current US state sexual assault laws and why some believe changing them will help alleged victims. The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
content: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers. The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day. Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement. In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction. A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed. "Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart." Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added. In parliament, the prime minister accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of seeking to "sow chaos" ahead of presidential elections in seven months' time. President Emmanuel Macron is nearing the end of his second and final term in office and LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently runner-up in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally. Macron was due to chair a meeting with ministers at the Élysée Palace on Tuesday evening to assess the situation. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said that from the start he had appealed for dialogue rather than school blockades and complained that "ultra-violent elements infiltrated the high-school student movements". He is now under pressure to respond to the students' demands. What has been offered, including a website for students to express their grievances and an afternoon of internal discussion in schools on Friday, has made little impression so far. There seems little chance of the protests coming to an end just yet. France's biggest union, the CGT, has said that further protests involving school and university students are being planned for Thursday. There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases. One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability". Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone. On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens. Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired. The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks. What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too. Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September. Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing. "We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling. Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris. The adventurer is nearing the end of his 28-year journey home to Hull from Chile. The demonstrators are calling for better government investment in high schools. The prefect of Pas-de-Calais says the 15-year-old's life is "not in danger" after the "very serious" incident. Two women were also rescued and taken to hospital with serious burns from the mixture of gasoline and seawater. Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some high schools after clashes between riot police and student protesters, France's education minister says. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The protests also have significant political implications, with the government accused of using excessive force and the opposition calling for greater investment in education.
